name: らーめん 鶴武者 (Ramen Tsurumusha)

claims.text: In-house wheat noodles are made daily on the shop's own noodle machine, so the kitchen is a wheat-heavy environment.
The seasoning/tare and items like the house menma are soy-sauce (shoyu) based; Japanese soy sauce is typically brewed with wheat.
All broth is animal-based (whole chicken plus pork bones and vegetables) and the tare includes dried scallop; toppings include pork chashu. No vegan/vegetarian option exists.
No preservatives and no chemical seasonings (MSG) are used, reflecting an explicit safe-for-the-whole-family ethos.
Child seats and child cutlery are provided and children are actively welcomed.

name: 料理屋 てら戸 (Ryouriya Terado)

claims.text: The signature noodles are wheat and the curry dipping broth is described as having a thick wheat-flour consistency.
A kappo serving sashimi and grilled fish; no wheat-free soy sauce or seasoning is indicated, so standard wheat-based soy sauce should be assumed.
The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles (sourced from the Kyoto noodle maker Teigaku) in a pork-bone broth; ramen tare of this style is wheat-based shoyu, so the dish contains wheat throughout.
Broth is pork-bone based and toppings include wagyu beef tendon, pork chashu, and fried chicken; no plant-based preparation is offered, so cross-contact with animal products is total.

name: セアブラノ神 slurp (Seabura no Kami slurp)

claims.text: The tsukemen tare is described as a blend of two soy sauce varieties cut with kombu-infused water; standard soy sauce is wheat-based.
The dipping broth is a pork-bone and chicken-collagen base finished with Iberico pork belly, and the bowl is topped with pork belly and sous-vide pork chashu — animal-based throughout.
Wheat is pervasive: gyoza, shumai and spring-roll wrappers, Chinese noodles, and fried-rice/stir-fry seasonings all involve wheat, with shared woks and fryers typical of a town-Chinese kitchen.
Dishes are seasoned in the Chinese-Japanese style; standard soy sauce/seasonings contain wheat. No wheat-free seasoning is indicated.
Pork is used throughout (gyoza, shumai, fried rice, noodle dishes) and stir-fries share oil and pans, so genuine vegan separation is not provided.
Cooking is intentionally light on garlic and heavy oil — a gentler, cleaner style of Chinese food, though this is about palate rather than allergen safety.
The chuka-soba broth is a soy-based (shoyu) chicken stock; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat.
On-site hand-pulling of Sanuki udon means heavy wheat flour use in the kitchen, with airborne flour and shared boiling water creating cross-contamination risk for any wheat-sensitive diner.
The ramen tare is built on a soy sauce infused with the shop's udon dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the seasoning base is not gluten-free.

Broth is chicken-bone stock plus bonito (katsuo) dashi and kombu, and the yuzu ramen is finished with pork back fat; evening menu centers on wagyu shabu-shabu and sukiyaki, so animal products are pervasive.

name: 担担 四条本店 (Tantan Shijo Honten)

claims.text: Tantan-men is built on wheat noodles with a sesame broth and a soy/miso-based meat tare that conventionally contains wheat; no gluten-free preparation is offered or noted.
The bowl is topped with pork meat miso and uses an animal-based broth/tare; no vegan or vegetarian version is available.
